explanations.answer: By good conduct done in humility
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. James says to show it "by his good conduct, by deeds done in the humility that comes from wisdom." Wisdom gets proven by what you do, not by what you say about yourself. A box that says "world's best cookies" still has to be opened and tasted.

James doesn't say a word about winning arguments here, friend. He points to "good conduct" and "deeds done in the humility that comes from wisdom." Winning an argument mostly proves you can talk louder than the other person. A humble life is how wisdom shows up.

Nope, James never mentions a spot at the front. He says the wise and understanding person shows it "by his good conduct, by deeds done in the humility that comes from wisdom." Standing up front doesn't make anybody wise, friend. It just gives everybody a good view of what you do.

Right on, baker. James says that kind of wisdom "does not come from above, but is earthly, unspiritual, demonic." It's wisdom that never looked up. It stays down here with the jealousy and the selfish ambition.

James says nothing about age or experience, friend. He says this wisdom "does not come from above, but is earthly, unspiritual, demonic." So the problem isn't that it's new. The problem is where it comes from.
That's a fun description, but it isn't the one James uses. He calls it "earthly, unspiritual, demonic." He never says clever or foolish. He just says it doesn't come from above.

Yes, baker. James says "where jealousy and selfish ambition exist, there will be disorder and every evil practice." Picture two people in one kitchen who both want to be head cook. Flour everywhere, and nobody is making cookies.

Sadness is a fair guess, friend, but it's not the word James uses. He says "there will be disorder and every evil practice." The word is disorder. Where jealousy and selfish ambition live, things come apart.

James doesn't talk about money in this verse, baker. He says "where jealousy and selfish ambition exist, there will be disorder and every evil practice." The missing word is disorder. Jealousy and selfish ambition bring a mess with them.

You spotted it, baker. James's list for the wisdom from above is "pure, then peace-loving, gentle, accommodating, full of mercy and good fruit, impartial, and sincere." Ambitious isn't on it. Selfish ambition shows up earlier, in the heart that has bitter jealousy (James 3:14).

Gentle is actually on the list, friend. James says the wisdom from above is "pure, then peace-loving, gentle, accommodating, full of mercy and good fruit, impartial, and sincere." The one that doesn't belong is Ambitious. Selfish ambition is what James warned about back in verse 14.

That one's right there on the list, baker. The wisdom from above is "full of mercy and good fruit." The one James never puts on it is Ambitious. Selfish ambition belongs to the earthly kind of wisdom.
James says the opposite, friend. The wisdom from above is "impartial." That means no favorites. It treats people the same.
Right, baker. James lists the wisdom from above as "impartial." It doesn't play favorites. The list also includes "sincere," so there's no act and no angle.
Yes, baker. James says "Peacemakers who sow in peace reap the fruit of righteousness." You plant peace and you get that harvest back. It's the opposite of the disorder he just warned about.

James doesn't say regret here, friend. He says "Peacemakers who sow in peace reap the fruit of righteousness." Peace is the seed, and righteousness is the fruit. Sow peace and you get the good harvest.

Praise from people doesn't come up in this verse, baker. James says "Peacemakers who sow in peace reap the fruit of righteousness." What they harvest is righteousness. Whether anyone claps isn't part of it.

True, baker. James asks, "What causes conflicts and quarrels among you? Don't they come from the passions at war within you?" He points inside, not outside. The fight starts in the heart before it reaches anybody's mouth.

James says the opposite, friend. He asks, "What causes conflicts and quarrels among you? Don't they come from the passions at war within you?" So the source is within them. He doesn't point at the other person.
That's it, baker. James says, "you ask with wrong motives, that you may squander it on your pleasures." They did ask. It was the reason behind the asking that was off.

explanations.answer: They give up asking too soon
explanations.explanation: James says they do ask, friend, so quitting early isn't the issue. He gives the reason: "you ask with wrong motives, that you may squander it on your pleasures." The trouble is the motive behind the asking.

Fasting never comes up in these verses, baker. James says, "you ask with wrong motives, that you may squander it on your pleasures." The reason is their motives. He doesn't mention anything they skipped doing first.

Yes, baker. James says "friendship with the world is hostility toward God." That's strong language, and I think James meant for it to land. He follows it with "whoever chooses to be a friend of the world renders himself an enemy of God."
James doesn't call it a test, friend. He says "friendship with the world is hostility toward God." Hostility is the word. He isn't being gentle about it.

James says nearly the opposite, baker. He says "friendship with the world is hostility toward God." Not a gift, and not something to hold onto. He says whoever chooses it "renders himself an enemy of God."
True, baker. Right after the hard question, James says, "But He gives us more grace." The heavy words aren't the last word. Grace comes next.
James says the opposite, friend. After the hard question about the Spirit and envy, he goes right on: "But He gives us more grace." So the next thing he says is about grace.
You got it, baker. The Scripture says, "God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble." James is pulling that from Proverbs 3:34. Same line, two kinds of people, and the humble get the grace.

Strength doesn't come up, friend. The Scripture James quotes says, "God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble." It's about proud and humble, not strong and weak. The grace goes to the humble.
Success isn't the test here, baker. James quotes, "God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble." The line is about pride and humility. A big trophy shelf doesn't come into it.
Right, baker. James says, "Resist the devil, and he will flee from you." It comes right after "Submit yourselves, then, to God." So the resisting happens alongside submitting to God.
James doesn't promise a harder fight, friend. He says, "Resist the devil, and he will flee from you." The devil flees. That word is the promise.
That's not what James says, baker. He says, "Resist the devil, and he will flee from you." Flee means he runs off. He isn't parked somewhere watching.
True, baker. James says, "Draw near to God, and He will draw near to you." That's a promise, and it comes with an invitation. You take a step and He draws near.
James says it plainly, friend: "Draw near to God, and He will draw near to you." So when they draw near, He draws near too. It's a promise, not a maybe.

James actually says it the other way around, friend. He says, "Turn your laughter to mourning, and your joy to gloom." So it's laughter turning into mourning, not the reverse. It's a serious call, and I think it's meant to make them stop and take their sin seriously.

Right, baker. James says, "Grieve, mourn, and weep. Turn your laughter to mourning, and your joy to gloom." It's a hard word, and it comes right after he tells them to cleanse their hands and purify their hearts. I'm a stamper who loves a good laugh, but I take this one soberly.

That's the word, baker. James says, "Humble yourselves before the Lord, and He will exalt you." Humbling comes first, and the lifting up is His part. It matches the grace for the humble back in verse 6.
James doesn't use test here, friend. He says, "Humble yourselves before the Lord, and He will exalt you." The word is exalt. For the humble, that's a promise.
Correct is a fair guess, baker, but it's not James's word. He says, "Humble yourselves before the Lord, and He will exalt you." Exalt means lift up. That's what He does for the humble.
Yes, baker. James says, "if you judge the law, you are not a practitioner of the law, but a judge of it." You were supposed to be doing the law. Instead you've moved over to the judge's chair.

Teacher is a nice guess, friend, but James doesn't say it. He says, "you are not a practitioner of the law, but a judge of it." The word is judge. The problem is stepping out of doing and into judging.

Student isn't the word, baker. James says, "you are not a practitioner of the law, but a judge of it." So he's talking about a judge. A student would still be learning, and a judge has already taken a seat.

explanations.answer: The One able to save and destroy
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. James says, "There is only one Lawgiver and Judge, the One who is able to save and destroy." He alone holds both the law and the verdict. That's why he follows it with "But who are you to judge your neighbor?"

explanations.answer: The One able to build and plant
explanations.explanation: James doesn't put it that way, friend. He says the one Lawgiver and Judge is "the One who is able to save and destroy." Building and planting aren't in the verse. Save and destroy are the words.

explanations.answer: The One able to heal and restore
explanations.explanation: Those are good words, baker, but they aren't James's. He says, "There is only one Lawgiver and Judge, the One who is able to save and destroy." The words are save and destroy. That's how he describes the only One who gets to judge.
